frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons and is positioning itself as a durable gas supplier to Europe. External pressure over supply volumes, pricing, and emissions rules remains a source of strategic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya challenges Algeria's border security and regional mediation role. Foreign military and commercial involvement in the Sahel narrows Algiers' room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lenders and firms remain deeply embedded in Angola's infrastructure and resource economy, although Luanda is diversifying partners. Debt servicing and project terms can constrain policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons still dominate export earnings and fiscal capacity despite efforts to expand critical minerals, agriculture, and refining. Foreign operators retain a major role in offshore production and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border blockade
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger continue to affect trade through the Port of Cotonou and the regional transport corridor. Political tensions and border insecurity expose Benin's logistics economy to decisions made beyond its territory.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea pressure
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening maritime surveillance and port security as it seeks to protect commercial flows and offshore interests. Dependence on external naval assistance creates both capacity gains and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its diamond reserves and market position to secure a larger domestic share of value, including sorting, cutting, and marketing. The challenge is preserving leverage as global diamond demand and prices face structural pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Battery-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are pursuing Botswana's copper, nickel, and other mineral prospects as the country seeks diversification beyond diamonds. Licensing and infrastructure decisions will determine whether new projects generate sovereign value or reproduce enclave extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal gold contest
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production and marketing while informal networks, armed groups, and foreign buyers compete for access. Insecurity limits the state's ability to convert mineral wealth into stable public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security partnership
frictionVectors.details: Expanded Russian military cooperation gives Ouagadougou an alternative to Western security ties but increases dependence on an external actor. The arrangement may strengthen regime survival while complicating diplomatic access, sanctions exposure, and resource-governance transparency.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA–DRC SECURITY RIFT
frictionVectors.details: Burundi's alignment with Kinshasa and its military role in eastern DRC expose it to retaliation, border instability, and pressure from competing regional blocs.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL GOVERNANCE GAP
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed nickel and rare-mineral projects offer revenue potential, but weak regulatory capacity and opaque licensing limit effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's strategic Atlantic location attracts U.S., European, and Chinese interest in maritime security and logistics, creating balancing pressures for Praia.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM–INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign tourism, imported energy, and externally financed port and airport infrastructure leaves the economy vulnerable to outside shocks and creditor leverage.

highlights: Oil, gas, and timber remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Persistent separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest undermines transport, agricultural production, and state legitimacy while complicating foreign investment.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-SECTOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and major infrastructure projects rely heavily on foreign capital and contractors, limiting domestic value capture and increasing governance risks.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY–MINING NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security forces has strengthened regime protection but risks transferring influence over gold and diamond assets without transparent public returns.

frictionVectors.title: REBEL CORRIDOR FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and cross-border networks continue to disrupt roads, trade routes, and mining zones, leaving Bangui with limited practical control beyond major urban centers.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND FISCAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on oil exports and foreign operators constrains fiscal autonomy, while volatile prices and opaque revenue management weaken the state's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL–SUDAN SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Sudan and the wider Sahel strains Chad's border security and humanitarian systems, while external powers compete for access and influence after changes in the French military presence.

frictionVectors.title: French-linked Mayotte dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French control of Mayotte, while migration enforcement and economic dependence keep relations tense. The dispute limits Comoros's room for maneuver with Paris and the EU.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Infrastructure and port development rely heavily on foreign donors and Gulf-linked capital. This creates opportunities for connectivity but constrains domestic control over strategic assets.

highlights: Mineral sovereignty collides with armed conflict
Western and Chinese interests remain entrenched

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral dependency
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains tied to foreign capital, processing capacity, and export corridors, limiting value capture inside the country. Kinshasa is seeking more leverage through contract reviews and local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and border pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and regional actors continues to disrupt territorial authority and mineral governance in the east. External military, diplomatic, and commercial involvement complicates efforts to consolidate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on oil exports, leaving fiscal sovereignty exposed to price volatility and offshore-sector partners. Limited diversification weakens domestic bargaining power over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have delivered major infrastructure but increased dependence on external creditors and contractors. Repayment pressures can narrow policy autonomy and affect control of strategic projects.

highlights: Cocoa and mining value capture under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire retains strong regulatory influence over cocoa but remains exposed to foreign traders, processors, and global price-setting mechanisms. Efforts to expand domestic processing are improving sovereignty over value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and other investors compete for ports, railways, energy, and mining projects. Abidjan can extract better terms from this competition, but strategic assets remain substantially foreign-financed.

highlights: Foreign bases fund sovereignty but constrain it

frictionVectors.title: Multi-power basing environment
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The revenue and security benefits are substantial, but competition among patrons limits independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: External financing and foreign-linked operators remain central to port, rail, and logistics infrastructure. Dependence on a narrow regional trade corridor and debt servicing reduces domestic control over long-term infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to treat Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam as a strategic water-security threat. Negotiations remain vulnerable to escalation during drought or unilateral reservoir operations.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and asset sales provide crucial fiscal support but increase outside influence over strategic land, ports, and infrastructure. Debt-service pressure constrains Cairo's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields are reducing export leverage, while opaque contracts and weak transparency limit domestic capture of remaining resource value. The state is seeking new upstream partners and downstream projects.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and energy interests remain important to Malabo's development model. Concentrated external financing increases vulnerability to repayment terms and politically conditioned investment.

highlights: Red Sea geography drives strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide essential revenue but leave Eritrea dependent on foreign operators, capital, and commodity prices. Limited transparency and sanctions concerns complicate long-term resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract regional and extra-regional security interest. Tensions with Ethiopia and competition around Red Sea access could draw the country into wider strategic bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African corridors
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South Africa for ports, energy connectivity, imports, and market access. This limits independent control over critical supply chains and exposes the kingdom to regional disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Investment and governance conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Textile, sugar, and manufacturing sectors depend on external buyers, regional trade preferences, and foreign capital. Governance concerns can affect market access while incentives may shift value toward outside firms.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains central to Ethiopia's electricity and sovereign-development strategy but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan. Seasonal filling and drought conditions could trigger renewed diplomatic or security pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and strategic finance
frictionVectors.details: Debt negotiations and reliance on Chinese, Gulf, and multilateral financing limit Addis Ababa's room to dictate infrastructure and resource terms. Conflict-related instability further weakens control over transport, mining, and energy assets.

highlights: Oil and manganese remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-control renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value addition in oil, manganese, and timber. This strengthens sovereign leverage but creates uncertainty for established French and other foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: External balancing
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is diversifying beyond France through ties with China, the Gulf states, and regional partners. Limited fiscal space and dependence on foreign capital constrain the pace of this strategic rebalancing.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential strategic partner
Tourism and fisheries face sovereignty pressures

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade routes, food supplies, energy links, and security cooperation. This provides stability but narrows Banjul's room for independent infrastructure and resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and weak monitoring continue to threaten local fisheries and maritime revenue. Limited enforcement capacity leaves the country vulnerable to extractive arrangements with overseas fleets.

highlights: Gold remains the core sovereignty asset

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage rivers, farmland, and public legitimacy while linking local networks to international gold markets. The state is attempting tighter formalization and enforcement but has struggled to overcome entrenched political and commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are competing for Ghana's lithium and other emerging mineral opportunities. Ghana is pursuing domestic processing and stricter licensing, but financing needs and IMF-era fiscal constraints weaken its bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is bringing major Chinese and international capital, rail, and port infrastructure into Guinea. The project could transform state revenue, but foreign control of financing and logistics creates long-term dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: Military rule and contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses mining renegotiations and local-content demands to assert sovereignty while delaying a credible democratic transition. Political uncertainty raises the risk of sanctions, project interruptions, and opaque resource deals.

highlights: Bissau port and fisheries remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine-trafficking networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime surveillance leave Guinea-Bissau vulnerable to use as a transit point for cocaine moving toward Europe. Trafficking networks erode state authority and can distort security and political decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign access to fisheries and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign vessels and concession arrangements capture much of the value from fisheries, while the country remains dependent on outside partners for port and transport investment. Limited administrative capacity restricts enforcement of national resource rights.

highlights: Debt and mineral sovereignty in focus

frictionVectors.title: Mombasa corridor and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is expanding port, rail, and energy links while balancing Chinese commercial interests, Western lenders, and domestic debt constraints. Control remains largely sovereign, but refinancing needs limit policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: New interest in Kenya's green-energy and mineral potential is increasing pressure for transparent licensing and local value addition. Foreign investment could accelerate development while reviving concerns over opaque concessions.

highlights: Small economy tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains the dominant buyer, financier, and infrastructure partner for Lesotho's water exports. Delays, compensation disputes, and unequal bargaining power continue to constrain Lesotho's control over a nationally critical resource.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-sector concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned industrial diamond operations provide exports and jobs but leave Lesotho exposed to external capital, commodity cycles, and limited domestic processing. Local beneficiation remains weak.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia relies heavily on foreign mining companies for capital, rail access, and export infrastructure. The government is seeking better fiscal returns and local processing without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and surrounding logistics networks attract competing foreign commercial interests. Weak domestic infrastructure leaves Liberia dependent on external operators and lenders for strategic connectivity.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to use production sites, export terminals, and budget flows as leverage. International operators and foreign governments retain substantial influence over access, investment, and disruption risk.

frictionVectors.title: Militia and foreign security presence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed armed actors and private military networks complicate national control of territory and energy assets. Fragmented authority makes infrastructure vulnerable to blockades, coercion, and opaque contracting.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt project exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operations connect Madagascar to global battery supply chains but remain highly dependent on foreign finance, technology, and export markets. Price volatility and environmental costs challenge the state's ability to capture durable value.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and local legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Roads, ports, and energy systems serving mining projects can strengthen national infrastructure while concentrating benefits around foreign-led enclaves. Land disputes and community concerns remain a recurring sovereignty risk.

frictionVectors.title: RUTILE AND RARE-EARTH CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is courting foreign investors to expand mining, but weak bargaining power and fiscal stress raise concerns that future projects will deliver limited domestic value. Regulatory capacity and community benefit-sharing remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: IMPORT-DEPENDENT INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Fuel, fertilizer, electricity, and transport systems remain exposed to external financing and regional supply disruptions. Chinese and multilateral-backed infrastructure provides access but increases long-term repayment and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The junta has replaced much of its former Western security relationship with Russian military support, narrowing diplomatic options while tying sovereignty claims to an external security provider. Insecurity continues to constrain state control outside major population centers.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONTRACT CONFRONTATION
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and stronger local processing requirements from foreign operators. Disputes risk production interruptions, arbitration, and pressure on already fragile public finances.

frictionVectors.title: GAS EXPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project strengthens Mauritania's bargaining position but leaves the country dependent on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure, and cross-border coordination with Senegal. Revenue management and local-content delivery will determine whether gas improves sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND RAIL BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore remains dependent on external markets, foreign technical expertise, and the national rail corridor to the coast. Chinese and Gulf-linked investment can expand capacity while reinforcing exposure to commodity cycles and infrastructure concentration.

frictionVectors.title: CHAGOS SOVEREIGNTY SETTLEMENT
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue recognition of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing relations with the United Kingdom and the United States. The Diego Garcia military facility remains the central constraint on full control of the territory.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE FINANCE SCRUTINY
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong commercial and legal institutions but faces continuing pressure from international tax and anti-money-laundering regimes. External compliance demands can narrow policy space in its financial-services sector.

frictionVectors.title: WESTERN SAHARA RESOURCE DIPLOMACY
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is using phosphate exports, renewable projects, and Atlantic infrastructure to consolidate its position in Western Sahara. The strategy generates diplomatic and legal friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and states wary of legitimizing contested resource control.

frictionVectors.title: EUROPEAN DEPENDENCE BALANCE
frictionVectors.details: Automotive, energy, agriculture, and logistics links with Europe provide substantial leverage but also expose Morocco to regulatory and trade pressure. Rabat is diversifying toward the Gulf, China, and Africa to reduce dependence without sacrificing access to European markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liquefied natural gas projects remain dominated by multinational capital and export contracts, limiting near-term domestic value capture. Security conditions and project delays continue to weaken Maputo's bargaining position.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity in Cabo Delgado threatens gas infrastructure, transport corridors, and state authority. Rwanda-backed and regional security deployments provide containment but deepen reliance on external security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil discoveries and established uranium exports are attracting major foreign operators, creating revenue opportunities but raising concerns over fiscal terms, local processing, and environmental oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen, port, and rail plans depend heavily on European and Gulf-linked financing and technology. Namibia is seeking stronger domestic ownership and value addition while avoiding excessive strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is asserting greater control over uranium and other extractive assets, challenging long-standing French commercial influence. Renegotiation risks production disruption, legal disputes, and reduced investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and closer ties with Russia and regional partners have increased Nigerien policy autonomy but reduced intelligence and logistical support against jihadist groups.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Finance
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain important to production and investment, while the government seeks greater national control through regulatory reform and domestic participation. Pipeline vandalism, theft, and insecurity continue to erode effective sovereignty over output.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Electricity, rail, ports, and digital infrastructure rely substantially on foreign contractors, lenders, and equipment suppliers. These dependencies accelerate development but expose Abuja to financing conditions and strategic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Networks
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security role and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo generate intense diplomatic and sanctions pressure. Kigali presents its posture as border security, while critics view it as enabling external resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong state direction over strategic projects but remains reliant on foreign aid, concessional finance, and international investors. Donor scrutiny over regional security policy could narrow its fiscal and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe has not established commercially viable oil production, limiting immediate resource leverage. Future offshore licensing could increase exposure to external energy firms and neighboring maritime claims.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign finance and partners for ports, energy, and tourism infrastructure. This creates strategic vulnerability despite the absence of a major extractive project.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production offers Senegal greater fiscal capacity but has intensified scrutiny of contracts involving international operators. Renegotiation efforts risk disputes with investors and delays to output.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing and mining competition
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing, phosphates, gold, and emerging gas infrastructure continue to generate concerns over foreign access and local benefit-sharing. Coastal communities remain sensitive to perceived depletion and weak enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign maritime influence
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances security and infrastructure relationships with India, China, and other external partners. Port access, surveillance, and maritime cooperation require careful management to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and tourism exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends on foreign-linked tourism and distant-water fisheries, leaving it vulnerable to market concentration and environmental degradation. Sovereign control is relatively strong, but enforcement capacity is limited by scale.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore operations and associated rail and port infrastructure provide revenue but leave the state exposed to foreign capital, commodity cycles, and concession disputes. Local-content and revenue-sharing demands remain politically significant.

frictionVectors.title: Port and mineral corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, logistics, and mining projects can improve connectivity while concentrating control over strategic corridors. Weak oversight raises concerns about opaque terms, environmental costs, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign offshore energy partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Turkey and other external actors are positioned to influence Somalia's emerging offshore petroleum sector. Federal-state disputes and limited regulatory capacity could leave future revenues vulnerable to unequal agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Competing port and maritime patrons
frictionVectors.details: UAE-linked port interests, Turkish security ties, and Somaliland's independent external relationships compete across Somalia's maritime space. These arrangements provide infrastructure and protection but deepen fragmentation of sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: POWER-SECTOR DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity and transmission constraints weaken industrial autonomy and increase reliance on private capital, imported technology, and emergency generation.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals, creating pressure over beneficiation and export policy.

frictionVectors.title: OIL-TRANSIT VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on pipeline access through Sudan, leaving public revenue and export capacity vulnerable to Sudan's war, infrastructure damage, and external commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: SECURITY-SECTOR FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Elite competition and incomplete security integration limit sovereign control over oil regions, transport corridors, and border trade.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND ARMS NETWORKS
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and foreign-linked trading networks continue to shape gold production, smuggling routes, and access to hard currency outside effective civilian oversight.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE FRAGILITY
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Port Sudan, oil-export infrastructure, and humanitarian corridors, increasing leverage for external security patrons and commercial intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: MEGA-PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, energy, and gas projects bring strategic connectivity but also deepen exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and other external financiers and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: MINING VALUE-CHAIN PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking more local processing and state participation in gold, graphite, and critical minerals, while investors resist tighter terms and export controls.

frictionVectors.title: PORT-DEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's role as a regional transshipment and logistics hub strengthens state revenue but leaves critical infrastructure exposed to foreign operators, financiers, and trade-cycle shocks.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: The state retains a central role in phosphate resources, yet limited domestic processing and external market dependence constrain full sovereign control over value creation.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European trade, tourism, and financial support while resisting external conditions linked to migration control and governance.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported Algerian energy and limited domestic generation capacity leaves Tunisia exposed to supply, pricing, and infrastructure pressures.

highlights: Oil infrastructure locks in external partnerships

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to export ambitions but faces environmental scrutiny, legal opposition, and financing constraints involving Western institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and lenders retain a major role in roads, energy, and industrial projects, increasing Kampala's infrastructure options while creating long-term repayment and control concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is attracting competing United States, European, Gulf, and Chinese interest in copper and cobalt, creating opportunities for diversification but risking renewed enclave extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages threaten mining sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower constraints and dependence on regional electricity imports weaken the government's leverage over mining operations and industrial value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese and Gulf mining influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors dominate key lithium, platinum, gold, and diamond projects, while weak transparency and limited domestic processing reduce Zimbabwe's share of resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment-system isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance push Harare toward alternative partners, increasing dependence on opaque bilateral deals and non-Western capital.
